title: Kierkegaard's individual
hook: each person stands before God alone, not as part of a crowd

segments.voice: Yesterday, Schleiermacher: religion beginning in the feeling of absolute dependence. Your line was entirely held. Whose hands did you name at your meal? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-three.

A stadium rises to its feet, and people are standing before they've decided anything. A group chat piles onto someone, and it's oddly easy to add one more laughing face. A crowd can carry a person a long way without asking them a single question. In Copenhagen, the Danish writer Søren Kierkegaard watched this happen in the newspapers, in the streets, and, he thought, in the churches too. So he did something odd for an author. He dedicated some of his books not to a crowd of readers, but to one: that single individual, whoever you are, reading alone. Today, Kierkegaard's individual.

Kierkegaard had a sharp sentence for it, usually put in English as: the crowd is untruth. He didn't mean people in groups are bad. He meant a crowd lets each person hide. In a crowd nobody quite decides; everyone just goes along, and nobody quite answers for it. Against the crowd he set a picture from the Bible: each person standing before God, alone. Paul writes to the Romans: "So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God." Every one. Of himself. Not as a member of a nation, a family, or even a congregation. In Fear and Trembling he dwells on Abraham, on the mountain, called by name, and answering, "Here am I." No committee. One voice, one answer. Kierkegaard wasn't against church or neighbors. He wrote a whole book, Works of Love, about loving the neighbor. His point was that nobody can hold your faith for you. Growing up in a country that called itself Christian, he thought, didn't make anyone a Christian by itself; each person had to become one, with their own yes. Some Christians find this bracing. Others worry it leaves too little room for the church as one body, and they point out how often scripture says "we." Both readings are alive today. But the picture he left is hard to shake: before God, there's no back row to hide in.
screen: `THE CROWD IS UNTRUTH` · `EACH ONE GIVES ACCOUNT` · `ABRAHAM: HERE AM I` · `NO BACK ROW BEFORE GOD`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: decide one thing yourself. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a small choice that's been waiting: a call to return, an invitation to answer, a habit you keep mostly because everyone around you does. Set aside, for a moment, what the group would say. What do you think? Not the loudest answer. Yours. You don't have to act on it yet. Just let it be your own decision, made with your eyes open. If you pray, you can bring it before God with Abraham's answer: here am I. The bell holds the time.
Kierkegaard's individual. The Danish writer's picture of each person standing before God alone: answerable, seen, not hidden in a crowd.

Your line: before God, alone. Today, when you notice yourself going along with a crowd, in a meeting or a group chat, pause for one breath and ask what you actually think. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Christians shaped by Kierkegaard often stress personal decision and honest self-examination before God, alongside life in a church; his books are read by Protestants, Catholics and readers of no faith.

fork.setup: the whole room is nodding along to something you're not sure is true. what does Kierkegaard's individual do?
options: nod too; the crowd is probably right.
stop, and answer for yourself, as before God.
walk out and never join anything again.
fork.reveal: the crowd is untruth, he said, because it lets each person hide. but he also wrote Works of Love: the point is standing on your own feet, not leaving people.

original.note: Greek, Romans 14:12: each one — "every one of us shall give account of himself to God."

trapdoor: what you thought: Kierkegaard said go it alone and skip church.
what it means: each person answers to God for themselves; nobody can hold your faith for you.
what a scholar hears: Kierkegaard put pen names on many books, but signed his upbuilding discourses himself and dedicated them to that single individual, his reader.

notes: 'The crowd is untruth' is a paraphrase of a common English rendering (from the essay on 'that single individual' attached to The Point of View); no quotation marks used. Confirm.
Dedications 'to that single individual' (Danish 'hiin Enkelte') appear in several of Kierkegaard's works; script says 'some'. Confirm.
Kierkegaard's critique of 'Christendom' summarized as 'growing up in a country that called itself Christian didn't make anyone a Christian by itself'; confirm fair.
Trapdoor: 'much of his work under pen names' (e.g., Johannes de Silentio for Fear and Trembling); confirm phrasing.
Practice borrows Abraham's KJV answer 'Here am I' (Genesis 22:11) as a line to say, not a new prayer.
Editor: hook no longer tells the listener what they did; cut the stock line 'here's what's easy to miss'; trapdoor 'much of his work under pen names' softened to 'some of his books'.

Audit: review asked about loosening a grip, which day 1262's carry no longer contains; now asks about the meal. 'Kept returning to Abraham' (unsourced) tied to Fear and Trembling. Garbled trapdoor floor rewritten; confirm the signed upbuilding discourses carry the 'hiin Enkelte' dedication.
